`HttpClient` is only an API surface; the actual HTTP work is done by a per-platform engine, and that engine artifact has to be declared in each platform source set.

### Which engine each target gets
- Android — `ktor-client-okhttp`, or `ktor-client-android` over `HttpURLConnection`.
- iOS and macOS — `ktor-client-darwin`, a wrapper around `NSURLSession`.
- JVM desktop — `ktor-client-cio`, or OkHttp again.
- Browser, JS and Wasm — `ktor-client-js` over `fetch`.
- Tests — `ktor-client-mock`, declared in `commonTest`.
- `commonMain` gets only `ktor-client-core` plus the plugins you install.

### What the build does when you forget one
`HttpClient { }` with no engine argument resolves whatever engine is on the classpath **at runtime**. Miss the artifact and nothing fails at compile time — the first request throws `IllegalStateException: Failed to find HTTP client engine implementation in the classpath`. So the Android CI job is green and the iOS app dies on its first screen.

Two shapes are common. Either rely on that discovery — engines declared per source set, `HttpClient { }` written once in common — or declare `expect fun httpClient(): HttpClient` and return `HttpClient(Darwin)` and `HttpClient(OkHttp)` from the actuals. The explicit one turns a missing target into a compile error and gives you somewhere to put engine-specific settings, which you will eventually want.

Rule of thumb: timeouts, retries and content negotiation belong in common code; the engine belongs in the leaf source set.

`commonMain` sees only the Kotlin standard library, so every `java.*` type is simply invisible there, and the gaps are filled by small official multiplatform libraries.

### Date and time — kotlinx-datetime
- `java.time.*`, `Date`, `SimpleDateFormat` and `System.currentTimeMillis()` are all JVM-only.
- kotlinx-datetime supplies `LocalDate`, `LocalDateTime`, `LocalTime`, `TimeZone`, `DateTimePeriod` and `DateTimeUnit`, plus serializers for them.
- `Instant` and `Clock` moved into the standard library in Kotlin 2.1.20: kotlinx-datetime 0.7.0 dropped its own, and 0.7.1 kept the `kotlinx.datetime` names alive as typealiases for `kotlin.time.Instant` and `kotlin.time.Clock`. Import the `kotlin.time` ones in new code.
- "Now" is `Clock.System.now()`. Elapsed time is `TimeSource.Monotonic.markNow()` — never two wall-clock reads, which an NTP sync can make negative.

### Files and bytes — kotlinx-io
- There is no `File`, no `InputStream`, no `java.nio`. `kotlinx-io-core` gives you `Buffer`, `Source`, `Sink`, `Path` and `SystemFileSystem` — Okio's shape, donated and made multiplatform. Ktor 3 rebuilt its own I/O on top of it.
- Okio 3 is still a fine alternative and is multiplatform too.

### The rest of the JVM habits
- `synchronized`, `ReentrantLock` and `ThreadLocal` → `Mutex` from coroutines, or the stdlib atomics.
- `UUID` → `kotlin.uuid.Uuid` in the stdlib; `Uuid.random()` is stable as of Kotlin 2.4, only the explicit `generateV4`/`generateV7` still need an opt-in.
- `String.format` → string templates; `Regex` and `kotlin.math` are already common.
- `BigDecimal` has no common equivalent — a third-party library or `expect`/`actual`.

The mental model: `commonMain` is the intersection of every target, not the JVM minus a few things.

`body<T>()` only deserializes; deciding that a response is an error is a separate job, and Ktor does not do it for you by default.

### Wiring JSON in
- Build exactly one `Json` in `commonMain` and hand it to `install(ContentNegotiation) { json(appJson) }`.
- `ignoreUnknownKeys = true` is not optional in a shipped app — the day the backend adds a field, every screen throws. `explicitNulls = false` matches how most APIs actually behave with missing keys.
- On the way out, `setBody(dto)` needs `contentType(ContentType.Application.Json)`; without the header the converter is never asked to encode and you send a string.

### Why the 502 explodes inside `body()`
- `expectSuccess` defaults to `false`, so a 502 is an ordinary response and execution walks straight into deserialization.
- ContentNegotiation picks a converter by `Content-Type`. Nothing is registered for `text/html`, so you get `NoTransformationFoundException` — an exception that mentions neither the status code nor the URL.
- A JSON body of the wrong shape throws `JsonConvertException` wrapping a `SerializationException`. Two very different causes, two exceptions no UI can act on.

### Where it belongs
Set `expectSuccess = true` so non-2xx throws `ClientRequestException` (4xx) or `ServerResponseException` (5xx) before anything is parsed, then translate every case once in `HttpResponseValidator { handleResponseExceptionWithRequest { … } }` into a sealed domain error the repository returns. Both apps then branch on the same Kotlin type instead of on engine exceptions that differ between OkHttp and Darwin.

Rule: status first, body second. Code that calls `body<T>()` before it knows the response succeeded is one bad gateway away from a crash.

Model it as a `@Serializable sealed` hierarchy: the compiler plugin registers the subclasses for you, and `Json` writes and reads a class discriminator to tell them apart.

### Closed polymorphism — the sealed case
- The base is a `sealed interface` or `sealed class` annotated `@Serializable`, and every subclass is `@Serializable` too.
- Give each subclass an explicit `@SerialName("post")`. Without one the discriminator value is the fully qualified class name, so moving the class to another package — or R8 renaming it on Android — silently changes your wire format.
- The discriminator key defaults to `"type"`. Change it per hierarchy with `@JsonClassDiscriminator("kind")`, or globally with `classDiscriminator` on the `Json`.

### Open polymorphism
A non-sealed base — an interface or abstract class whose implementations live in other modules — has to be registered by hand in a `SerializersModule` with `polymorphic(Base::class) { subclass(Impl::class) }`. Nothing scans anything: there is no classpath scanning, no service loader, and on Kotlin/Native no `Class.forName` to fall back on, so an unregistered subtype is a `SerializationException` at runtime on every target. That is exactly why sealed hierarchies are the default advice — the plugin keeps the registry so you cannot forget an entry.

### Two traps
- A subclass with a real property named `type` collides with the discriminator, and `Json` rejects the whole hierarchy the first time it is used. Rename the property or the discriminator.
- If the server sends no discriminator at all, a `JsonContentPolymorphicSerializer<Base>` picks the serializer by looking at which fields the object has.

Mental model: sealed means the compiler owns the registry; anything else means you own it.

SQLDelight generates plain blocking code, the driver is the only per-platform piece, and every generated call executes on whatever thread you happened to call it from.

### One database, three drivers
- Android — `AndroidSqliteDriver(AppDatabase.Schema, context, "app.db")` on top of `SupportSQLiteOpenHelper`; the file lands in `/data/data/<pkg>/databases/`.
- iOS and the other native targets — `NativeSqliteDriver(AppDatabase.Schema, "app.db")` over SQLiter, which puts the file in the app's Documents directory by default. That directory is backed up to iCloud, so a large rebuildable cache belongs under Library instead — pass `onConfiguration` to move it.
- JVM tests — `JdbcSqliteDriver(JdbcSqliteDriver.IN_MEMORY)`, and you must call `AppDatabase.Schema.create(driver)` yourself, because there is no open helper doing it behind your back.
- Wire it as `expect class DriverFactory`, or build the driver in each app and inject it.

### The thread
`executeAsList()`, `executeAsOne()` and `transaction { }` all block. There is no Room-style compile-time check, no strict mode on iOS, and a JVM test with an in-memory database is far too fast to reveal it. Wrap every read and write in `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` — that dispatcher exists on Kotlin/Native as well as the JVM — and keep transactions short, because SQLite serialises writers and one long transaction stalls every other coroutine touching the file.

Rule of thumb: the driver is platform code and you write it once; the dispatcher is the thing you have to remember at every call site.

A `.sq` file describes the schema a *fresh* install gets; upgrading an existing database is a separate `.sqm` file, so editing only the `.sq` leaves old installs with old columns and new queries that select from them.

### The two kinds of file
- `.sq` — the current `CREATE TABLE` statements plus the labelled queries. Always the destination state, never a history.
- `.sqm` — one migration per file, named for the version you are migrating **from**: `1.sqm` takes a v1 database to v2. `AppDatabase.Schema.version` is the highest migration number plus one.
- The driver runs `Schema.create` on a brand-new file and `Schema.migrate(old, new)` on an existing one. `AfterVersion(3) { driver -> … }` hangs a data backfill off a specific step.

### Making the build catch it
Set `schemaOutputDirectory` and `verifyMigrations = true` inside the `sqldelight { databases { … } }` block. The `generate<SourceSet><Name>Schema` task snapshots the current schema as `<version>.db`; commit that file. `verifySqlDelightMigration` then replays every `.sqm` against the snapshots and fails when the result does not match the `.sq` — and it hooks into `check`, so CI already runs it. That is the gate that would have caught this change.

### The SQLite you actually get
`ALTER TABLE … RENAME COLUMN` needs SQLite 3.25 and `DROP COLUMN` needs 3.35, and the version is whatever the OS shipped — old Android devices have neither, and it differs from iOS. The portable migration is still create-new-table, `INSERT … SELECT`, drop, rename.

Rule of thumb: a `.sq` edit without a matching `.sqm` only breaks on upgrade — the one path a fresh install off `main` never exercises.

`asFlow()` registers a `Query.Listener` for the tables the query reads, and SQLDelight notifies those listeners only when a write goes through the generated API on the same driver.

### How the pipeline works
- `queries.selectAll().asFlow().mapToList(io)`, from `app.cash.sqldelight:coroutines-extensions`. `asFlow()` emits `Query` objects, not rows; `mapToList` is what actually executes them, and the `CoroutineContext` you pass is where that blocking execution happens — pass `Dispatchers.IO`, never the main dispatcher.
- It emits once immediately on collection, then again after every notifying write.
- Notification granularity is the table, not the row. Any insert into `player` re-runs every query reading `player`, so add `.distinctUntilChanged()` to stop identical lists re-rendering.
- Inside `transaction { }` notifications are held until the outermost commit, so a batch of twenty inserts produces one emission, not twenty.

### What silently fails to notify
- A statement executed straight on the driver, or any raw SQL, because nothing tells the listener registry which tables changed. This is the usual cause of a frozen list.
- A second driver over the same file. The registry is in memory and per driver, so two drivers on `app.db` are two databases that never hear each other — and a write from another process or an app extension is invisible for the same reason.

Rule: one driver per database per process, every write through the generated mutators, and the mapping context is a dispatcher you chose deliberately.

Swift never talks to Koin directly: you start the container from a top-level Kotlin function the iOS app calls once, and expose typed accessors, because `get<T>()` is `inline reified` and reified generics do not survive the Objective-C bridge.

### Starting the graph
- `commonMain` declares the modules; anything platform-shaped — the SQLDelight driver, secure storage, the Ktor engine — goes behind `expect fun platformModule(): Module`.
- Wrap the start in `fun initKoin(extra: KoinAppDeclaration = {}) = startKoin { extra(); modules(sharedModule, platformModule()) }` so both apps share one definition of "the graph".
- Android calls it from `Application.onCreate` with `androidContext(this)`; `koin-android` then gives you `by viewModel()`.
- iOS calls a **no-argument** wrapper such as `fun doInitKoin() { initKoin {} }` from the `App` initializer or `AppDelegate`, because Swift sees neither Kotlin default arguments nor a trailing `KoinAppDeclaration` lambda.
- Call `startKoin` twice and you get `KoinAppAlreadyStartedException`. SwiftUI previews and test hosts are where that happens.

### How Swift resolves anything
`get<T>()` is inlined at the call site and has no runtime existence, so it never appears in the generated Objective-C header. Resolve on the Kotlin side instead: a Kotlin `object` implementing `KoinComponent`, with one plain function per thing iOS needs. Swift then writes `Deps.shared.feedViewModel()` and gets a concrete class back.

Keep that object down to a handful of ViewModels rather than every repository. The DI graph is an implementation detail of the shared module, and every extra exported type is one more entry in a header both the compiler and your Swift colleagues have to read.

A container buys you lifetimes, one override point, and a lookup the iOS side can call without spelling out a twelve-argument constructor — until you need those, hand-written factories are a legitimate DI story and cheaper to read.

### What manual wiring already gives you
- Constructor injection, checked by the compiler. A missing dependency is a build error, not a runtime `NoBeanDefFoundException`.
- No extra klib, no reflection, and nothing new to explain to the iOS team — a graph object is just a Kotlin class exported to Swift like any other.
- Fakes in `commonTest` are trivial: you already pass everything in.
- The cost is bookkeeping. Every singleton is a `by lazy` you maintain by hand, and the platform still has to feed in the parts only it can build — the SQLDelight driver, the Ktor engine, the Keychain wrapper.

### What the container adds
- Named lifetimes: `single`, `factory`, and scopes tied to a session or a screen, instead of hand-rolled laziness.
- One place to swap an implementation. A test starts the same modules plus a module that overrides `FeedApi`.
- A resolution entry point, which is what iOS wants: Swift calls a small Kotlin facade that does `get()`, rather than assembling the graph in `AppDelegate`.
- The price is that wiring errors move to first use. Koin 4.x can verify a module in a test, but that check runs on the JVM — it does not protect the iOS build.

Koin is the multiplatform default; kotlin-inject and Metro do the same job with KSP at compile time; Hilt and Dagger are JVM-only and stay in `androidMain`.

Rule of thumb: wire by hand until the platform apps can no longer spell the constructor call, and whichever you pick, hide it behind a facade so Swift never imports the container.

`multiplatform-settings` is the right default for preferences and the wrong home for a token, because the guarantees a secret needs cannot be expressed by `putString(key, value)`.

### What the library actually is
- A common `Settings` interface with a platform implementation under it: `SharedPreferencesSettings` on Android, `NSUserDefaultsSettings` on Apple, plus a DataStore-backed one and an experimental `KeychainSettings`.
- `ObservableSettings` gives you change flows, which is what makes it pleasant for a theme, a last-used tab or a cached feature flag.
- None of the standard backends encrypt anything. `NSUserDefaults` is a plist and shared prefs are XML on disk.

### Where the abstraction leaks for a secret
- A Keychain item has an accessibility class — `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly` versus the default that syncs and survives a restore. There is nowhere to say that through a key-value API, and the default is the wrong one.
- Keychain items outlive app deletion, so a "logged out" user can come back logged in after a reinstall unless you clear on first run.
- On Android, Jetpack Security's `EncryptedSharedPreferences` is deprecated; the durable answer is a Keystore-backed key you encrypt with, holding ciphertext in DataStore.
- The API shape is wrong too: Keychain calls can fail and can block, so you want `suspend` and a real error, not a synchronous getter that returns null for both "absent" and "device locked".

Put the token behind a `TokenStore` interface in `commonMain`, implement it per platform, inject it, and fake it in `commonTest`. Keep the boring keys in `Settings`. The line to hold: shared code owns the refresh logic, the platform owns the storage.

`expect`/`actual` is a compile-time switch with no seam: it binds one name to exactly one implementation per target, so anything you might want to fake, configure or swap belongs behind an interface instead.

### What it is genuinely good for
- Tiny leaves with one obvious implementation each and nothing to test: a device model string, a UUID, a locale-aware formatter.
- `actual typealias`, which maps an expected declaration onto a type that already exists on the platform — zero wrapper code.
- Completeness the compiler enforces. Add a target and the build fails until every `actual` exists, which is exactly what you want for a leaf.

### Why it stops scaling
- There is no fake. `commonTest` cannot supply an `actual`, so a common test of anything sitting on an `expect` really exercises the JVM implementation, and the iOS one is only covered by an iOS test run.
- One implementation per target and no more — no in-memory variant, no per-flavour choice, no decision at runtime.
- Growth is N declarations times M targets of files, and every new target blocks the build until all of them are written.
- `expect class` in particular is still beta; the compiler warns about it unless you pass `-Xexpect-actual-classes`, and the members have to match exactly, so refactoring one hurts in three places at once.

The shape that scales is an interface in `commonMain`, implementations in `androidMain` and `iosMain`, and the choice made once where the app is assembled — DI, or a single `expect fun` factory if you want to keep the platform wiring invisible.

Rule of thumb: if you can imagine wanting a fake of it, it is an interface; if it is a one-line call into the platform, `expect`/`actual` is fine.

The Kotlin Gradle plugin generates them from the targets you declare, through the default hierarchy template — so the target list defines the tree, and adding one silently changes what the shared parents have to compile for.

### How the tree gets built
- `applyDefaultHierarchyTemplate()` creates the intermediate sets — `nativeMain`, `appleMain`, `iosMain`, `watchosMain` — above the per-target leaves, and the plugin applies it for you as long as you never write a `dependsOn` edge by hand.
- A group only materialises if you declared targets in it. `iosMain` exists because you declared iOS targets, not because a folder with that name is on disk; a directory the template did not create is not part of any compilation, and the build log says so.
- Write one explicit `dependsOn` and the template steps aside for the whole project — the log tells you it was not applied, and from then on the tree is yours to maintain.

### What the new target broke
- `appleMain` now compiles for watchOS as well, and watchOS has no UIKit. Apple-shared code that reached for `UIDevice` has to move down into `iosMain`.
- Every `expect` in `commonMain` needs an `actual` covering the new leaf.
- Every dependency declared in an ancestor set must publish a klib for the new target, or resolution fails there.

Dependencies come from the version catalog as one coordinate per library — `libs.ktor.client.core`, not a per-platform artifact — because Gradle module metadata picks the right variant for each target. The catalog is also where the Kotlin version and every compiler-plugin library stay pinned together; a mismatch there breaks far louder than an ordinary version bump.

Swap the network for Ktor's `MockEngine` in `commonTest` and make sure the backoff `delay` runs on the test scheduler — then `runTest` skips it in virtual time and the virtual clock itself becomes the assertion.

### Faking the backend
- `ktor-client-mock` is multiplatform, so the fake engine lives in `commonTest` and the same test runs on the JVM and on the simulator.
- `MockEngine { request -> ... }` is called for every attempt, retries included. A counter in the closure lets you answer `respondError(HttpStatusCode.ServiceUnavailable)` twice and then a real body.
- The trap: a success response needs `headers = headersOf(HttpHeaders.ContentType, "application/json")` or `ContentNegotiation` refuses to deserialize it and you debug the wrong failure.
- The handler is also where you assert on the request — `request.url.encodedPath`, headers, `request.body.toByteArray()`.

### Making the waiting virtual
- `runTest` only skips a `delay` that runs on its own `TestScheduler`. The engine has its own dispatcher, so a delay executed inside the client's machinery can genuinely sleep.
- The reliable version is to keep the backoff in your own suspend code, which inherits the test's context. If you use the `HttpRequestRetry` plugin instead, give it a delay hook in tests and record what it asked for rather than serving it.
- Then assert the shape, not just the outcome: attempts made, and `testScheduler.currentTime` equal to the sum of the backoff steps.

Never assert timing with a real clock or a `withTimeout` guard; a test that passes because the machine was fast is a test that fails on CI.

On Android the shared code is ordinary JVM bytecode and Crashlytics deobfuscates it from your R8 mapping file; on iOS it is native machine code, so the report is only as readable as the dSYM you uploaded — and by default the Kotlin exception itself never reaches the reporter.

### Android
- Shared classes are in the same DEX as the app, so an uncaught exception arrives with its Kotlin frames intact.
- The Crashlytics Gradle plugin uploads the R8 mapping automatically; if someone turned `mappingFileUploadEnabled` off for speed, every release build after that is unreadable.
- Handled failures in shared code go through `recordException`, which is a non-fatal, not a crash.

### iOS
- Kotlin/Native emits a `.dSYM` next to the framework. With `isStatic = true` the symbols end up in the app's own dSYM instead — either way that file has to be uploaded, from the archive, by the Crashlytics run script or `firebase crashlytics:symbols:upload`. A CI job that discards the archive is the usual reason for hex frames.
- Release binaries carry only light debug info; `-Xadd-light-debug=enable` is the switch that keeps function names in the trace.
- An uncaught Kotlin exception crossing to Objective-C terminates the process, and the report blames the Kotlin/Native runtime rather than your `IllegalStateException`. Install `setUnhandledExceptionHook`, report `stackTraceToString()` yourself, then call `terminateWithUnhandledException` so the crash still lands.

Practically: define one `CrashReporter` interface in `commonMain`, implement it with Crashlytics on Android and hand in a Swift implementation on iOS (or use Sentry's KMP SDK, which ships both). Treat the Kotlin-side hook as the source of truth and the native crash report as corroboration.

A KMP publish is not one artifact but one module per target plus a root module whose Gradle metadata points at them — and none of it helps an Xcode consumer, who needs an XCFramework published alongside.

### What comes out
- A root `shared` module with a `.pom` and a `.module` file listing every variant. Consumers write one coordinate and Gradle resolves `shared-jvm`, `shared-android` or `shared-iosarm64` per target.
- Per-target modules carrying the real artifacts: jars for JVM and Android, `.klib` for each native target, plus sources.
- klibs are readable only by a compatible Kotlin compiler, so your Kotlin version is part of your public contract — say it in the release notes and bump deliberately.
- The iOS *app* team consumes none of that. They take an `.xcframework`, as an SPM binary target with a checksum or as a Pod, built in the same release job.

### What a break costs
- JVM and Android consumers recompile against a new jar, so a `@Deprecated` shim gives them a migration window.
- The iOS consumer compiles Swift against generated Objective-C headers. A rename, or a parameter added to an existing function, changes the selector — a source break with no source of yours to patch. Kotlin's `@Deprecated` does export (WARNING becomes deprecated, ERROR and HIDDEN become unavailable), and it is the only warning they get.
- Anything `internal` never reaches the header, and `@HiddenFromObjC` removes a public declaration from it — a small exported surface is what keeps you free to refactor.

Gate it in CI with a committed ABI dump — the binary-compatibility-validator, or the Kotlin Gradle plugin's own ABI validation — so a removal fails your build instead of theirs.

Gradle resolves a separate compile classpath per target, so a JVM-only dependency fails at *resolution* for the native target — "no matching variant", listing the attributes it wanted — long before anything is compiled or linked.

### Reading the failure
- The message prints the variants the library does publish (`apiElements`, `org.jetbrains.kotlin.platform.type = jvm`) against what the consumer asked for (`native`, plus `konan.target = ios_arm64`). That is the whole diagnosis: it ships no klib for your target.
- A transitive offender looks identical except the coordinate named is not the one you added — a multiplatform library pulling in a JVM-only dependency for its JVM variant only is fine; one doing it from common code is not.
- To know before you type the coordinate: look at the library's `.module` metadata on Maven Central, or search klibs.io, which indexes multiplatform libraries by target.
- Real *link* failures read differently — `Undefined symbols for architecture arm64` from a missing cinterop or framework, not a resolution error. If Gradle got that far, the dependency was fine.

### Your options
1. Keep it out of `commonMain`: an interface in common, the SDK wired in `androidMain`, an iOS implementation from the platform side. Say this one first — it is usually right anyway.
2. Replace it with a multiplatform equivalent: Ktor for OkHttp, kotlinx-datetime for a JVM date library, Kermit for Timber.
3. Port it, if it is a small pure algorithm rather than a platform integration.
4. Leave the feature native on iOS and share only the model.

Not options: an `iosMain` stub that throws — it compiles and then ships — or switching `implementation` to `api`, since variants are attribute-matched, not scope-matched. The invariant to state out loud: `commonMain` may depend only on libraries publishing a klib for every target you build.
